back: The fraction of lookups answered by the cache. Average latency = hit ratio × hit cost + (1 − hit ratio) × miss cost.

front: Going from 90% to 99% hit ratio does what to database load?
back: Cuts it ten-fold: misses drop from 10% to 1% of reads.
The data actively used over a period. If it fits in the cache, the hit ratio is high even when the full dataset is huge.

front: Rough cost: in-process lookup vs distributed cache lookup?
back: About 100 ns to a few µs in process; about 0.2–1 ms for one in-data-centre round trip to Redis or Memcached.

front: The two biggest jumps on the latency ladder?
back: In-process to any network hop (about 1,000×), and in-region to cross-continent (100× or more).
Keep this response for a year and don't revalidate. Used for fingerprinted static assets whose URL changes when content changes.

front: Why do static assets get a content hash in the file name?
back: You can't delete a response from users' browsers. A new version gets a new URL, so the old cached copy is simply never requested.
Only the user's browser may cache the response; shared caches like CDNs and proxies must not.

front: Three problems with in-process caches on many servers?
back: Duplicated memory per server, values that diverge between servers, and an empty cache after every deploy.
A small in-process cache with a short TTL in front of a distributed cache. Absorbs the hottest keys and protects hot Redis nodes.

front: Fix for many sequential cache calls per page?
back: Batch them: MGET in Redis or multi-get in Memcached, so one round trip fetches many keys.
The database's in-RAM cache of data pages: shared_buffers in PostgreSQL, innodb_buffer_pool_size in MySQL InnoDB.

front: Why is a buffer pool hit slower than an app cache hit?
back: The database still parses, plans, locks and executes the query; only the disk read is skipped.

front: Three properties of good cache candidates?
back: Read far more than written, expensive to produce, tolerant of slight staleness.

front: What must a cache key include?
back: Everything that changes the response: user ID for personal data, locale, permissions, API version. Missing a field can leak one user's data to another.
